passages.title: Hitting the Wall: Where the Marathon Is Really Decided
passages.source: Jeremy Lee's Boston Marathon pacing-decay analysis
passages.text: Hitting the Wall: Where the Marathon Is Really Decided. "The wall" is not a myth or a metaphor. It is a measurable inflection point in pace, and the data pinpoint where it happens. **What the Boston data show (31,655 finishers):** - Pace stays roughly flat through about **20 km**. - From **~30 km** onward, pace climbs steeply. A clear, population-wide inflection. - Median late-race (35–40 km) slowdown is **15%**. - **27%** of finishers slowed by more than **25%** in the closing kilometers. **The effect scales with finish time:** - Sub-3:00 runners stay nearly flat to the finish. - Runners at 4:30+ commonly slow **30% or more** late in the race.

passages.title: Even Pacing Strategy
passages.text: Even Pacing Strategy. to a hard course or a hot day. - Pick a pace you're confident you can hold for the *whole* distance, then run the first few miles a touch slower. **Executing it:** - Deliberately hold back in the opening 5–10 km when adrenaline makes goal pace feel easy. - Check splits, but race by effort as fatigue builds. - Aim to reach halfway feeling controlled, with pace still in reserve. **Actionable takeaway:** Set a realistic, condition-adjusted goal pace and run it evenly. Discipline in the first third, resisting the urge to bank time, is the strongest predictor of a strong finish.

passages.title: Even Pacing Strategy
passages.text: Even Pacing Strategy. For the vast majority of marathoners, **even pacing.** Holding a steady effort and pace throughout, produces the best result. A slightly negative split (finishing marginally faster) is the ideal ceiling, but even splitting is the practical target. **Why even pacing wins:** - Running too fast early burns glycogen and generates fatigue disproportionately, which you repay with a steep slowdown in the final 10–12 km. - **Banking time early is a trap.** Time gained by going out fast is almost always lost, with interest, late in the race. - A steady pace keeps energy expenditure efficient and delays the wall.
